newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. hopeful on info technology deal at trade meet.
newsitem.headline: U.S. hopeful on info technology deal at trade meet.

text.p: Progress in negotiating a global Information Technology Agreement (ITA) is making the United States hopeful that trade ministers will be able to endorse a pact next month, a senior U.S. trade official said on Tuesday.
Under the liberalisation pact, affecting an estimated $400 billion in trade, countries would agree to eliminate all tariffs on a range of electronic products by the year 2000.

Duties on computer hardware and software, semi-conductors, facsimile machines and other telecommunications products would be gradually repealed from next year. Tariffs would be taken to zero by century-end on a most-favoured-nation (MFN) basis.

"We are talking about products essential to the information super highway. Coverage is pretty extensive. It is a broad range which makes the super highway work," the senior U.S. trade official, who asked not to be named, told Reuters.

Negotiators from the four major trading blocs of the United States, European Union, Japan and Canada are in their second week of meeting bilaterally and with Asian and Latin American envoys to hammer out a draft accord.

Negotiators hope to sign a draft of the agreement at the World Trade Organisation's (WTO) first ministerial meeting of its 125 member states from December 8-13 in Singapore, where they will set the global trade agenda into the next century.
But the official said "We are pushing quite hard for an agreement in Singapore. I'd love to say we'll have a deal at the end of this week, but it is hard to imagine."

ITA negotiations had hit a snag earlier this year when the EU refused to discuss the accord, complaining that its exclusion from a U.S.-Japanese semiconductor deal signed in July would block European access to Japan's computer-chip market.

The United States and Japan have eliminated tariffs on semiconductors, while EU member states maintain an average tariff of seven percent. The United States imports about $100 billion of information technology equipment per year. Of that, 80 percent comes from Asia-Pacific nations.
The deadlock was broken at ministerial talks between the big trade powers in September in Seattle.
Now, the official said negotiators were still working on narrowing differences, expanding country participation and defining product coverage.
Defining product coverage is key because terms are outdated, and countries define the same product in different ways.
But lists have now been drawn up identifying a product by its harmonised system tariff number and by a description.
"You may classify a product in one category, and I may classify it in another. But regardless where it is classified, it will be subject to ITA," the U.S. official said.

"We've made progress in the Quad and have good endorsement by our partners in the Pacific," the U.S. official said, adding that the Quad countries had drafted a "working document" identifying products.

Also, "there is strong interest among the APEC (Asian and Pacific Economic Cooperation) countries who are critical to the agreement. We will be looking for APEC ministers to give a strong push to ITA when they meet later this month."
